bull_bear.body: - No buyback/dividend specifics discussed on call. Capital directed at greenfield/brownfield capacity build to capture commercial + naval pipeline. Order-book gap to be "stemmed" by NGC1 plus 20-25% of balance anvil orders.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- Order-book drawdown below INR 20,000 cr; near-term FY27/FY28 revenue/margin trough during NGC design phase (operating de-leverage risk flagged by analyst).
- NGC signing slipped from expected 31-Mar-2026 to Jun-2026 quarter — execution/timing risk on contract conversion.
- Margin sustainability dependent on whether write-backs recur; CMD non-committal on exact figure.
- Split-yard tenders (P-17B, MCMV, LPD, FAC) mean award is not guaranteed — competitive risk vs MDL/CSL/GSL.
- Commodity escalation/time delays for new (not-yet-signed) contracts; VDS (variable depth sonar) is a buyer-furnished developmental item (no financial liability to GRSE, but a program dependency).
bull_bear.title: Risks

bull_bear.body: Confident and detailed; CMD (Cmde Hari) gave granular order-by-order breakups and pipeline values. Notably candid that order book dropping below INR 20,000 cr is a positive (execution speed), and conservative on margin commitments ("will try to maintain," "can't say exact"). Reassured on his own continuity through FY27–FY28. Declined confidential weapon-fit questions.
bull_bear.title: Mgmt tone

bull_bear.body:
- Three warships delivered on a single day (claimed first in India's history) drove the large positive delta between 31-Mar provisional and final FY26 revenue — revenue recognition was held conservatively pending Navy liaison/handover.
- Defence Standing Committee report showed near-2yr contract value for warships/survey vessels dropping from ~INR 42,000 cr to ~INR 18,900 cr; CMD argued this reflects annual fund-outflow timing, not intent — AoNs and RFPs continue.
- NGC revenue is essentially a FY29 story, not FY28 — the "intermittent" gap is filled by OPV/commercial/research projects, not NGC.
- BEL contract for NGC electronics expected 3-6 months after GRSE signs prime contract — read-through for BEL order inflow.
- Conventional platforms defended as durable vs autonomous/drone narrative (armament, endurance >3 months at sea).
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious

bull_bear.body:
- customer lock-in: repeat warship builder for the Indian Navy and Indian Coast Guard — evidence: around 800 platforms built including 111 warships to Indian Navy, Indian Coast Guard, Govt. of Mauritius and Govt. of Seychelles, stated as the highest number of warships built and delivered by any shipyard in the country; eight warships delivered to the Indian Navy in FY26 — against it: the AR lists 'Large dependency on customers at every stage of shipbuilding' as a threat and notes L&T Shipbuilding and Shoft Shipyard repositioning themselves as warship builders
- scale: multi-yard shipbuilding capacity — evidence: four shipyards in Kolkata (three for shipbuilding, one for ship repair) with capacity for concurrent construction of 28 ships, to be raised to 32 platforms by end 2026 [planned] — against it: 'Constraints of a riverine shipyard due to limitations in the depth and width of navigable channels with effects of silting in rivers' and location in densely populated areas with narrow roads
- technology: in-house warship design and indigenisation — evidence: designed and built frigates, ASW corvettes, missile corvettes, fleet tanker and LST(L); 218 IPRs filed of which 117 granted; indigenous equipment fit above 90% on ASW SWC ships, 87% on Survey Vessels and 80% on P17A frigates
- resource (lease): concession over existing dry docks for ship repair — evidence: Concession Agreement with Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata signed 07 Oct 2021 for three dry docks of the Khidderpore Dry Dock complex, with one more dry dock being taken over
- integration: in-house engineering units supplying naval platform equipment — evidence: Deck Machinery Unit supplied over forty major equipment for new construction platforms; Diesel Engine Plant, Ranchi delivered, tested and commissioned all 28 of the 1 MW Diesel Alternators for the Indian Navy's P17A programme
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Board independence shortfall — key committees could not be constituted — The company discloses that due to non-availability of adequate Independent Directors, the CSR & SD, Stakeholders Relationship and Risk Management Committees were not reconstituted from 06 Apr 2025 to 31 May 2025, leaving risk oversight and shareholder-grievance committees unconstituted for that period.
- Physical limits of the existing Kolkata premises — The mission statement ties greenfield shipyards outside the Kolkata premises to the need to 'overcome limitations to build/repair/recycle ships upto 400,000 DWT', i.e. the company itself states that its existing Kolkata premises limit the size of ships it can build, repair or recycle.

outlook.body:
- NGC contract signing expected in Q1 FY27 (Jun-2026 quarter); "no red flags."

outlook.body:
- **Commercial / export shipbuilding:** entry via German 12-ship MPV; intends to follow with higher-margin, higher-value, complex hybrid/large vessels only. Strong European inbound interest.

outlook.title: Growth verticals

outlook.body:
- Brownfield and greenfield shipbuilding expansion on both the Western and Eastern seaboards, because even the enlarged Kolkata capacity is considered inadequate for defence and non-defence demand
- Pursue growth across warships, weapons, commercial vessels and green & autonomous technologies under the Vision 2035 roadmap towards Maharatna status
- Increase focus on repair and refitting of Indian Navy and Indian Coast Guard vessels, and build up the ship repair vertical including for foreign coast guards
- Leverage government initiatives (MIV 2030, MAKV 2047, SBFAS, SbDS, National Logistics Policy) to make a mark in commercial shipbuilding
- Innovation in autonomous platforms, green vessels and AI-enabled shipyard processes, supported by the GAINS start-up scheme
- Workforce training and leadership development to prepare for the projected six-fold growth in business
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Current shipbuilding capacity caters for concurrent construction of 28 ships; ongoing modernisation of existing Kolkata facilities is to raise this to 32 platforms by end 2026. Considering even that inadequate, GRSE has decided on brownfield and greenfield expansion on both seaboards: a shipyard at Raichak, West Bengal (closer to sea), with approvals expected in the current calendar year, infrastructure build-up from 2027 and three to five years to full operationalisation; and a full-fledged total ship solution facility on the Western Seaboard for shipbuilding, green ship recycling and ship repairs. The mission statement targets greenfield shipyards outside the Kolkata premises able to build/repair/recycle ships up to 400,000 DWT. Ship repair uses three existing dry docks of Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port under a concession agreement; capacity is also sought through collaboration with private shipyards, such as the MoU with Modest shipyard. A 250 kWp rooftop solar plant was commissioned at Ranchi during the year.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Indian naval modernisation pipeline exceeds Rs 2.3 lakh crore over a 10–15 year horizon into the mid-2030s
- Indian Navy and Indian Coast Guard each plan a fleet of 200 ships; their combined programme over the next 15 years indicates orders for more than 150 warships, giving long-term visibility rather than short-term spikes
- An estimated Rs 28,000–30,000 crore of Navy capital expenditure flows annually into shipbuilding and shipyard infrastructure; payments for large platforms are milestone-based and spread over 8–12 years
- Commercial shipbuilding presents an opportunity worth Rs 12,000–15,000 crore a year; Sagarmala objectives imply tripling the coastal and inland fleet, a potential demand of about 12.75 million CGT
- MIV 2030 targets operational waterways rising from 16 to 23 and cargo on them from 73 MT to over 200 MT per annum by 2030
- Government shipbuilding schemes (SBFAS, SbDS etc.) with a total corpus of around Rs 70,000 crore over the next 10 years aim to make Indian shipbuilders cost competitive
- Global ship repair market of about USD 55–60 billion by 2030; India's share is under 1% though 7–9% of global trade passes within 300 NM of its coastline
- Global shipbuilding market expected to grow from about USD 160–170 billion in 2024 to USD 200–230 billion by 2030, driven by fuel-efficient, low-emission and advanced vessels
- Global shipyards operating at capacity with rising demand for quality tonnage
- Competition: private shipyards such as L&T Shipbuilding and Shoft Shipyard are repositioning themselves as warship builders
- Order book of Rs 15,324.13 crore as on 31 March 2026, spanning nine projects and 39 platforms
- L1 bidder for the Next Generation Corvette project of approximately Rs 33,000 crore; contract signing will provide long-term revenue visibility
- Export contract with Carsten Rehder, Germany for four Multi-Purpose Vessels CORAL 7500 (Hybrid) valued at USD 62.44 million, taking the German order tally to twelve vessels
- Contract with the Geological Survey of India for two Coastal Research Vessels
- Construction commenced on hybrid ferries for the Government of West Bengal, a Trailing Suction Hopper Dredger for Bangladesh and an Acoustic Research Ship for NPOL-DRDO; keels laid for nineteen platforms during the year
- Follow-on order of Rs 211.68 crore secured for 30 mm Naval Surface Guns

deepdive.thesis: GRSE posted its best-ever year (FY26 revenue INR 7,002 cr, +38%; PAT INR 748 cr, +42%), executing fast enough to draw down its order book below INR 20,000 cr for the first time in 5 years. The investment case now hinges on order-book replenishment: a near-term NGC (Next Gen Corvette) contract worth ~INR 33,000 cr (L1, price negotiations complete, signing expected in Jun-2026 quarter) plus ~INR 1,50,000 cr of AoN-accorded RFPs on the anvil (excl. NGC). Margins have stepped up sharply (FY26 EBITDA ~11.6% vs FY25 ~8.3%), partly aided by provision write-backs; sustainability of double-digit margins through the NGC design-phase trough (FY27–FY28) is the key debate.

thesis: GRSE posted its best-ever year (FY26 revenue INR 7,002 cr, +38%; PAT INR 748 cr, +42%), executing fast enough to draw down its order book below INR 20,000 cr for the first time in 5 years. The investment case now hinges on order-book replenishment: a near-term NGC (Next Gen Corvette) contract worth ~INR 33,000 cr (L1, price negotiations complete, signing expected in Jun-2026 quarter) plus ~INR 1,50,000 cr of AoN-accorded RFPs on the anvil (excl. NGC). Margins have stepped up sharply (FY26 EBITDA ~11.6% vs FY25 ~8.3%), partly aided by provision write-backs; sustainability of double-digit margins through the NGC design-phase trough (FY27–FY28) is the key debate.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Indian naval modernisation pipeline exceeds Rs 2.3 lakh crore over a 10–15 year horizon into the mid-2030s
- Indian Navy and Indian Coast Guard each plan a fleet of 200 ships; their combined programme over the next 15 years indicates orders for more than 150 warships, giving long-term visibility rather than short-term spikes
- An estimated Rs 28,000–30,000 crore of Navy capital expenditure flows annually into shipbuilding and shipyard infrastructure; payments for large platforms are milestone-based and spread over 8–12 years
- Commercial shipbuilding presents an opportunity worth Rs 12,000–15,000 crore a year; Sagarmala objectives imply tripling the coastal and inland fleet, a potential demand of about 12.75 million CGT
- MIV 2030 targets operational waterways rising from 16 to 23 and cargo on them from 73 MT to over 200 MT per annum by 2030
- Government shipbuilding schemes (SBFAS, SbDS etc.) with a total corpus of around Rs 70,000 crore over the next 10 years aim to make Indian shipbuilders cost competitive
- Global ship repair market of about USD 55–60 billion by 2030; India's share is under 1% though 7–9% of global trade passes within 300 NM of its coastline
- Global shipbuilding market expected to grow from about USD 160–170 billion in 2024 to USD 200–230 billion by 2030, driven by fuel-efficient, low-emission and advanced vessels
- Global shipyards operating at capacity with rising demand for quality tonnage
- Competition: private shipyards such as L&T Shipbuilding and Shoft Shipyard are repositioning themselves as warship builders
- Order book of Rs 15,324.13 crore as on 31 March 2026, spanning nine projects and 39 platforms
- L1 bidder for the Next Generation Corvette project of approximately Rs 33,000 crore; contract signing will provide long-term revenue visibility
- Export contract with Carsten Rehder, Germany for four Multi-Purpose Vessels CORAL 7500 (Hybrid) valued at USD 62.44 million, taking the German order tally to twelve vessels
- Contract with the Geological Survey of India for two Coastal Research Vessels
- Construction commenced on hybrid ferries for the Government of West Bengal, a Trailing Suction Hopper Dredger for Bangladesh and an Acoustic Research Ship for NPOL-DRDO; keels laid for nineteen platforms during the year
- Follow-on order of Rs 211.68 crore secured for 30 mm Naval Surface Guns

capex_expansion.body: Current shipbuilding capacity caters for concurrent construction of 28 ships; ongoing modernisation of existing Kolkata facilities is to raise this to 32 platforms by end 2026. Ship repair uses three existing dry docks of Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port under a concession agreement; capacity is also sought through collaboration with private shipyards, such as the MoU with Modest shipyard. thesis: GRSE posted its best-ever year (FY26 revenue INR 7,002 cr, +38%; PAT INR 748 cr, +42%), executing fast enough to draw down its order book below INR 20,000 cr for the first time in 5 years. The investment case now hinges on order-book replenishment: a near-term NGC (Next Gen Corvette) contract worth ~INR 33,000 cr (L1, price negotiations complete, signing expected in Jun-2026 quarter) plus ~INR 1,50,000 cr of AoN-accorded RFPs on the anvil (excl. NGC). Margins have stepped up sharply (FY26 EBITDA ~11.6% vs FY25 ~8.3%), partly aided by provision write-backs; sustainability of double-digit margins through the NGC design-phase trough (FY27–FY28) is the key debate.
financial scorecard:
| Metric | Q4 FY26 | Q4 FY25 | YoY | FY26 | FY25 | YoY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue from ops (INR cr) | 2,119 | ~1,643 | +29% | 7,002 | ~5,074 | +38% |
| PAT (INR cr) | 303 | 244 | +24% | 748 | 527 | +42% |
| EBITDA margin | — | — | — | ~11.6% | ~8.3% | +~330 bps |
*Note: FY26 revenue cited as "best figures of 7,200" in one answer vs 7,002 stated in opening; opening 7,002 used as primary. Margin figures sourced from analyst Q&A and confirmed by mgmt. PYs derived from stated growth rates.*
guidance:
- NGC contract signing expected in Q1 FY27 (Jun-2026 quarter); "no red flags."
- NGC revenue recognition: nil in FY27; "mediocre" (design inputs) in H2 FY28; major chunk from FY29 (S-curve, ~65% of ship cost is equipment). Mgmt floated ~3-4-5% of NGC project cost recognised in FY28–29.
- FY27 revenue accrual to be "very healthy, in line with last 3-4 years"; declined to confirm FY28 will avoid a dip — depends on order intake.
- Margins: "will try to maintain similar margins" in FY27, FY28 and FY29 (i.e. ~11.5% region), but CMD would not commit to an exact number "only in the 1st Quarter."
- Capacity: 28 platforms now → 32 by end of CY2026 via in-premises modernization.
order book & pipeline:
- **Order book: INR 15,324 cr** (9 projects, 39 platforms). ~95% shipbuilding (INR 14,730 cr); non-defence now 22.5% of total.
  - P-17A frigate: INR 5,868 cr remaining (1 ship left, ~74% progress, delivery in CY2026)
  - ASW SWC: INR 2,035 cr (4 of 8 delivered; 2 at ~80%, 2 at ~60%; project to finish FY27)
  - NGOPV (4 ships): INR 5,168 cr (1st launching 20-May; completion FY29)
  - → Warship building total ~INR 11,361 cr
  - Non-defence: ORV INR 749 cr; Coastal Research Vessels (2) INR 260 cr; Acoustic Research Ship INR 456 cr; Hybrid Ferries (13) INR 207 cr; MPV (12, German export) INR 1,345 cr; Dredger (Bangladesh) INR 66 cr
- **On the anvil (AoN accorded, RFP/award pending) — total ~INR 1,50,000 cr excl. NGC:**
  - NGC: ~INR 33,000 cr (L1, signing imminent) — *not counted in the 1.5 lakh cr*
  - 7× P-17 Bravo frigates: ~INR 70,000 cr (split 4+3 between two yards, L1/L2); RFP expected within 3 months
  - 12× Mine Countermeasure Vessels: AoN ~INR 32,000 cr (split 8+4); RFP H2 FY27
  - 4× LPD: ~INR 35,000 cr (split 2+2); RFP H2 FY27
  - 120 Fast Interceptor Craft: ~INR 3,500 cr (split 80+40); RFP within 3 months
  - 31 Follow-On Water Jet FAC: ~INR 3,500 cr; RFP within 3 months
- **Live tenders:** 2× MPV ~INR 1,500 cr (bid submitted); 5× NGOPV Coast Guard ~INR 2,000 cr; 22× Interceptor Boats Coast Guard ~INR 1,000 cr.
- **Commercial (Ministry of Shipping aggregated demand):** 4 live tenders — 4 Platform Support Vessels (INR 1,200–1,500 cr), 4 MR tankers, 6 VLGCs, 6 Aframax vessels. Revitalization package ~INR 69,725 cr.
segment / subsidiary:
- Shipbuilding ~95% of order book; warships dominate value. Non-defence rose to 22.5% of order book (research vessels, ferries, export MPV, dredger).
- Bridges vertical crossed INR 200 cr revenue for first time (110 portable steel bridges delivered, incl. 30 export).
- Exports: >INR 270 cr revenue in FY26; active dialogue with European ship-owners shifting from China/Korea (capacity-full) to India on price + quality.
growth verticals:
- **Commercial / export shipbuilding:** entry via German 12-ship MPV; intends to follow with higher-margin, higher-value, complex hybrid/large vessels only. Strong European inbound interest.
- **Autonomous platforms:** separate "new technology" business vertical, started ~3.5 yrs ago across subsurface/surface/aerial. Subsurface & surface versions developed; one product already supplied to a DRDO org. Part of Make-I/Make-II; eyeing XL-AUV Make project to materialise in 3-5 years.
- **Bridges:** INR 200 cr+ milestone, export traction.
margins & cost:
- FY26 EBITDA margin ~11.6% (FY25 ~8.3%); analysts flagged Q4 FY25 & FY26 provision write-backs as a tailwind, pegging "sustainable" margins at ~9.5-10%. CMD repeatedly guided "similar margins" ahead without confirming the write-back-adjusted base.
- All current projects on fixed-price contracts; vendor/subcontractor orders also fixed-price and placed early → minimal commodity escalation impact. Steel/industrial-gas delays "very marginal, insignificant," absorbed. New bids will explicitly factor commodity/time uncertainty.
- ~65% of a ship's cost is equipment; in NGC, ~55-60% of that equipment value is electronics (weapons/sensors) — large share to BEL.
capex: - Expansion: 2 Brownfield yards (West Bengal) + 2 Greenfield yards (1 West Bengal, 1 Gujarat). In-premises modernization lifts capacity 28→32 platforms by end CY2026. Driven by govt shipbuilding revitalization package (~INR 69,725 cr) and Ministry of Shipping demand aggregation. No specific capex INR figure given on call.
capital allocation: - No buyback/dividend specifics discussed on call. Capital directed at greenfield/brownfield capacity build to capture commercial + naval pipeline. Order-book gap to be "stemmed" by NGC1 plus 20-25% of balance anvil orders.
risks:
- Order-book drawdown below INR 20,000 cr; near-term FY27/FY28 revenue/margin trough during NGC design phase (operating de-leverage risk flagged by analyst).
- NGC signing slipped from expected 31-Mar-2026 to Jun-2026 quarter — execution/timing risk on contract conversion.
- Margin sustainability dependent on whether write-backs recur; CMD non-committal on exact figure.
- Split-yard tenders (P-17B, MCMV, LPD, FAC) mean award is not guaranteed — competitive risk vs MDL/CSL/GSL.
- Commodity escalation/time delays for new (not-yet-signed) contracts; VDS (variable depth sonar) is a buyer-furnished developmental item (no financial liability to GRSE, but a program dependency).
mgmt tone: Confident and detailed; CMD (Cmde Hari) gave granular order-by-order breakups and pipeline values. Notably candid that order book dropping below INR 20,000 cr is a positive (execution speed), and conservative on margin commitments ("will try to maintain," "can't say exact"). Reassured on his own continuity through FY27–FY28. Declined confidential weapon-fit questions.
non-obvious:
- Three warships delivered on a single day (claimed first in India's history) drove the large positive delta between 31-Mar provisional and final FY26 revenue — revenue recognition was held conservatively pending Navy liaison/handover.
- Defence Standing Committee report showed near-2yr contract value for warships/survey vessels dropping from ~INR 42,000 cr to ~INR 18,900 cr; CMD argued this reflects annual fund-outflow timing, not intent — AoNs and RFPs continue.
- NGC revenue is essentially a FY29 story, not FY28 — the "intermittent" gap is filled by OPV/commercial/research projects, not NGC.
- BEL contract for NGC electronics expected 3-6 months after GRSE signs prime contract — read-through for BEL order inflow.
- Conventional platforms defended as durable vs autonomous/drone narrative (armament, endurance >3 months at sea).

themes.title: Naval shipbuilding & maritime
themes.need: A multi-decade naval order book and indigenous warship/submarine build, plus the naval-equipment supply chain (HVAC/chillers, mechanical seals, marine gearing) and maritime services, underpin the theme. GRSE carries a large RFP pipeline (~INR1.5 lakh cr referenced); SHREE REFRIGERATIONS 544458 supplies naval HVAC; SEALMATIC 543782 naval/submarine seals; ELECON defence-marine gearing; KMEW/SEAMECLTD/DREDGECORP maritime services.
themes.driver: Fresh MoD warship/submarine orders + naval-equipment indigenization inflow; maritime-infra/offshore contract wins.
